Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (418 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed.
  • Recent findings suggest that google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the newly introduced desktop search page after a successful test.
  • The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

Recent findings suggest that google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the newly introduced desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

The other significant change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”.

It has been revealed that it’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s new AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that shows that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

Sources indicate that this change indicates more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday described Russia's actions in Ukraine and Europe as an "irresponsible gamble" that would only increase European resolve. Trump said he could not speak about security guarantees for Kyiv because there was no peace deal in place to end Russia's ongoing invasion after over four and a half years.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius "welcomed in every respect" a move by Russian President Vladimir Putin to consult Europeans on the future of Ukraine (see entries below for more details).

During a trip to the Polish capital Warsaw, Pistorius added that declining such an invitation to Moscow would send the "completely wrong signal.".

"We need to talk. Only by talking can we ultimately achieve results," he stated.

Pistorius stated reaching an agreement was the goal — not simply sitting down in a room together.

"He [Putin] must now show that he truly means what he says and that he will then take the necessary steps to ensure that, at the very least, a ceasefire is established and that peace-sustaining stability can once again take hold in Europe," the German minister noted.

The comments came the same day a pair of Russian missiles and a drone were reported to have violated Polish airspace (see entries below).

While Russian officials remarked Germany, France and the UK had been invited to send representatives to talks on Ukraine, no details about a time or place for such talks have been confirmed.

"In our assessment, this case shows that Russian intelligence services attempted to carry out a targeted killing in Denmark," PET head Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen told a news conference.

Kieffer-Kristensen added that Russia was suspected of enlisting the help of a local criminal gang for the killing.

The Danish Foreign Ministry subsequently summoned the Russian ambassador and expelled the Russian Embassy's defense attache, Foreign Minister Lars ​Lokke ​Rasmussen stated.

The foreign minister also called on European countries to stop issuing visas to Russians and stated the Danish government would have taken harsher steps if Russia had a larger diplomatic presence in Denmark.

This week, Ukraine introduced a series of strikes on the Kerch bridge, which links occupied Crimea to mainland Russia.

The 19-kilometer (12-mile) bridge has both rail and roadways, part of which has been destroyed in the strikes.

The bridge is widely seen as a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014, and damage to it is regarded as a significant psychological blow to Moscow.

Following the strikes, Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate and warned the response would be "far more painful" than the damage Ukraine had caused to the Kerch bridge, as seen in the sliding image below.

At least 1,144 children were killed or injured in Ukraine during the first 10 months of 2026, the United Nations said.

UNICEF, the UN's children's agency, mentioned that between January and October, at least 114 children were killed and 1,030 injured.

The agency mentioned it was the highest number of casualties seen in more than 3 years.

"That is more than three children who have been killed or injured every single day" this year, stated UNICEF spokeswoman Louise Wateridge.

Last month alone, at least 146 children were killed or injured across Ukraine, the UN agency said.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called Russia's violation of Polish airspace "utterly unacceptable.".

"The incursion into ​Polish airspace is utterly unacceptable. I condemn it unreservedly," ​Burnham remarked at an EU-UK ​summit press conference ‌in Brussels.

The incursions were reported as Poland held military exercises involving the "Coalition of the Willing" that ​groups allies of Ukraine, including the UK.

British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting stated the move was a Russian provocation aimed at dividing Europe.

Recent findings suggest that "Europe ​will not be ‌deterred from our support for Ukraine," Streeting noted. "We will not allow ⁠Putin to divide our continent, and we recognise that the ⁠frontline ​in Ukraine is the frontline for freedom and democracy everywhere.".

Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov has reportedly invited representatives from Germany, France and the UK to Moscow for talks on the war in Ukraine, according to Russian news agency Interfax.

"We are waiting for a reply," the diplomat was reported to have said.

On Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said European officials would be invited to Moscow to discuss whether they should participate in US-led talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.

Interfax reported that Ryabkov stressed that such a visit would not automatically mean that European nations would be involved in the negotiations on ending the war on Ukraine.

A statement from the French president's office remarked Europeans were ready to visit Moscow if given a full role in Ukraine talks.

"Our requirement will be that the opening or formalisation of this dialogue clearly signify, from the Russian perspective, that Europeans have their full role in the negotiations and participate actively in the next round of talks with the United States and Ukraine," an advisor to President Emmanuel Macron told reporters. European leaders have been pushing for a seat at the negotiation table, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz saying on Thursday that the outcome of the war in Ukraine would determine European security for years to come.

The European Commission said it has released another €7.9 billion ($8.67 billion) ‌to ⁠Ukraine to support the country's finances and keep public administration running.

"Ukraine continues to deliver on reforms, while defending itself each and every day. Today, we are disbursing nearly €8 billion — this is the largest payment made so far," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen noted.

Sources indicate that "This makes it clear: real progress on reforms brings real results and benefits. As Ukraine perseveres and moves further on its European path, they can count on our support," remarked von der Leyen.

It’s the ninth disbursement of funds under the mechanism to support Ukraine.

With today's release of funds, the EU and its member states have provided €245.5 billion in overall support to Ukraine, which includes €3.8 billion from the proceeds of immobilized Russian assets.

The German Foreign Ministry has expressed its support for Poland after reports a Russian missile had entered Polish airspace.

Recent findings suggest that "Russian missiles have once again violated Polish airspace. This is part of Russia's ongoing provocations," Germany's Foreign Ministry said in a statement on X.

"Instead of signaling a willingness to negotiate, Putin is signaling the opposite: he is opting for confrontation," the post said.

"We stand firmly by our neighbor and NATO ally Poland," the statement concluded.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated he had spoken to Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk about what he called "grave violations of Polish airspace overnight.".

Rutte mentioned that NATO jets had been scrambled in response.

"We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend," Rutte said.

"This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine," the NATO chief mentioned.

"I condemn Russia's attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine," Rutte said.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot remarked that Paris had requested a UN Security Council meeting after Russia introduced one of the war's largest missile attacks on Ukraine.

According to recent reports, "The Kremlin has struck Kyiv again. Civilians have been killed," Jean-Noel Barrot stated on X.

On Thursday at the Coalition of the Willing talks in Berlin, French President Emmanuel Macron said that Ukraine needed to be able to defend itself and that allies needed to ensure Kyiv had the means to do so.

The government of Estonia remarked road border crossings with Russia would be shut from December 1 on security grounds.

"The closure ​of the border crossing points is not a reaction to a ​single incident, ‌but the next step following Russia's aggression against Ukraine and the increasing frequency of sabotage and hybrid operations in Europe," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stated in a statement.

The Kremlin has denied the allegations saying they're part of a pattern of false allegations against Moscow originating from European countries.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Estonia of  planning to erect a newly introduced "Iron Curtain" and mentioned it would respond.

"Should Tallinn proceed with these ‌plans, our country will take the necessary ‌political ​and diplomatic measures in response to safeguard its national interests," Zakharova told a press briefing in Moscow.

They asked founder Brewster Kahle to voluntarily recognize the union, but will go to an NLRB vote if needed.

Recent findings suggest that workers at the Internet Archive, home to the Wayback Machine, are unionizing. After signing up to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA), they're asking founder Brewster Kahle to voluntarily recognize the union. As a backup, they've filed for a National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) election. Kahle hasn't responded publicly yet.

Wired reports that over 80 of 124 eligible US workers signed on. None of their asks are radical: better pay, additional benefits that apply to everyone and paths for career development and promotion. Organizing committee member Danielle Leard tied the unionization campaign to the Internet Archive's mission, stating that job security, benefits and livable wages go "hand-in-hand with sustaining the Archive long-term.".

There's a recent precedent from another Bay Area nonprofit. Wikimedia Foundation workers joined the CWA in September, but only after the foundation refused to voluntarily recognize the effort and it went to an NLRB vote. Wikimedia workers ultimately voted in favor by a count of 158 to 14.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S.
  • The state is investigating the manufacturer to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public.
  • “The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.

The state is investigating the manufacturer to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public.

“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added.

The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).

The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, remarked earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position.

According to recent reports, the company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government.

The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is mentioned to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors.

In a recent development, democratic representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal.

“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.

Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that nikhil Gupta (seen in a 2024 courtroom sketch) pleaded guilty in a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a U.S. resident who advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.

A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

Sources indicate that nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge noted he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.

Sources indicate that india has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.

Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019.

He previously told the BBC that "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.

Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.

Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in Fresh York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.

Sources indicate that at his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors noted. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.

Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton stated in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.

Following Gupta's arrest, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs said that Yadav is no longer employed, external by the Indian government.

The country also set up an inquiry committee to address security concerns raised by the US, the spokesperson said.

Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.

Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".

"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed.".

India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.

Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.

In a victim impact statement to the court, Pannun mentioned the foiled assassination attempt has not deterred his activism.

"I am entirely willing to take India's bullets if that is the price required to achieve freedom," he wrote.

Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.

In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.

In a recent development, nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.

The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets.".

#58631. European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1318 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1318 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans.
  • The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
  • The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans.

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

According to recent reports, in confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

Recent findings suggest that if Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, stated she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik stated. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”.

Under the blueprint, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.

The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.

One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.

In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

It has been revealed that in order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

In a recent development, on this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.

The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.

During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

It has been revealed that timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, remarked the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

In a recent development, sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, noted the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.

She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”.

Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, remarked: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission mentioned the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.

It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.

Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

Germany news: Kids take to streets over school, climate and costs

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2408 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Below, you can review a roundup of the biggest headlines in Germany from Friday, November 20:.
  • Representatives of IG Metall, Germany's largest union, said Friday that thousands of union workers at dozens of factories around the country will continue to carry out 24-hour strikes in an effort to force employers to cough up a 5% wage increase as well as job guarantees.
  • Audi, BMW, Ford, Opel and Volkswagen are all in IG Metall's sights, as are shipyards in northern Germany.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Below, you can review a roundup of the biggest headlines in Germany from Friday, November 20:.

Representatives of IG Metall, Germany's largest union, said Friday that thousands of union workers at dozens of factories around the country will continue to carry out 24-hour strikes in an effort to force employers to cough up a 5% wage increase as well as job guarantees.

Audi, BMW, Ford, Opel and Volkswagen are all in IG Metall's sights, as are shipyards in northern Germany.

Companies say they cannot afford to pay wage increases and will have to slash benefits, site upgrades and hundreds of thousands of jobs in the automotive, electrical and mechanical engineering and metal production sectors.

They are instead offering a phased increase of 1.3% for 2028 — Germany's current inflation rate is hovering around 3%.

It is the first time the union and its 3.7 million members have turned to 24-hour strikes in eight years and they are hoping the move will offer them some leverage when collective bargaining talks begin next week.

IG Metall's northern coastal representative Daniel Friedrich said Friday: "Our members stand united behind our demands. On Monday, we will continue the 24-hour strikes at more companies.".

Police in the German state of Saxony say they deployed water cannons to Leipzig and used them on individuals who repeatedly shot fireworks at officers there after a large demonstration ended.

Police say roughly 2,500 people took part in a demonstration in Leipzig organized by the group Gen Z Takes Charge, far fewer than the estimated 7,000 who joined the first of these on October 31 (see entries below).

Across Germany, some 87,000 people joined in demonstrations, according to Gen Z Takes Charge.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday announced that Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani had pledged €15 billion ($16.5 billion) in latest German defense and technology investments.

During a Berlin press conference with the emir, Merz remarked, "This strengthens both of us, particularly in future technologies such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors and aviation.".

The Qatar-Germany collaboration is aimed at improving security and defense projects that also include defending against cyberattacks, with Merz saying, "We are particularly open to latest partnerships in the defense industry.".

That cooperation comes as both nations look to beef up defenses amid regional conflicts with global consequences.

The chancellor and the emir also stressed the fundamental importance of diplomacy in the resolution of conflict, with the two leaders' focused largely on Iran and the Middle East — and the need to get the flow of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz closer to pre-war levels.

The emir called for deescalation, saying, "We are convinced that true political resolution is the only way to achieve lasting peace.".

Merz added that the two agreed on the war in Ukraine, saying: "Russia must stop its time-wasting diplomatic games. Moscow has to finally sit down for real peace negotiations.".

Merz was straightforward on Iran, saying Germany wants peace in the Middle East because it needs affordable energy.

He later called out Russian maritime marauding on the Black Sea, labeling it a threat to global food security.

The German broadcaster Sky TV — not to be confused with the British-based Sky Sports F1 which is the largest English-language commercial F1 broadcaster — will not be sending any staff to the Formula 1 Qatar Grand Prix because of security concerns in connection with the conflict in Iran and the wider Middle East.

Sky TV declared the move on Friday, just a week before the contentious race weekend from November 27-29.

Sky will broadcast the entire race weekend as usual, but will use global feed images and will not send any of its own staff to Lusail International Circuit.

F1 races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia this spring were canceled as the US war with Iran was in its most active phase, with major disruptions to commercial flights.

The season-ending double header in Qatar and then the United Arab Emirates a week later has been in serious doubt ever since.

Nominally at least, both races are going ahead — and in all likelihood, teams will have already started dispatching equipment and personnel to the region to begin preparations by now.

Sky TV remarked it still planned to send a team to the season finale in Abu Dhabi, just across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, on December 6.

But it noted it continued to "monitor developments and assess the situation on an ongoing basis.".

Organizers of the Gen Z Takes Charge protest group spoke out about why they took to the streets again.

Co-organizer Akram Selo called on Germany's leadership to meet the young people's demands.

"Talks won't make us stop demonstrating," he told RBB-Inforadio in comments aired on Friday.

In a recent development, "Essentially, our demands should be addressed, and we should be given assurances. That is what needs to happen, not empty promises," Selo added.

Recent findings suggest that "So far, we feel that we aren't being taken seriously at all," he remarked. "The way we're being treated suggests that the aim is to sideline our demands and discriminate against us by focusing on other trivial matters.".

Another group, the alliance "School strike against conscription" held its own protest to demand an immediate halt to surveys about potential availability for the German Armed Forces, or Bundeswehr, that are currently non-binding and only obligatory for teenage boys.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stated Ukraine must ‌continue ⁠to ⁠push ahead swiftly with reforms, particularly ​on the rule of ​law and tackling ​corruption, ‌if it hopes to receive a prerequisite for further financial ‌aid and investment.

Merz made the comment at a ‌business ​summit in Berlin that was organized by the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce.

"It is now essential to press ahead with these reforms swiftly and resolutely —particularly, and I say this openly, with regard to the rule of law and corruption," Merz told attendees.

The German chancellor said that sustained reform efforts by Kyiv ​were necessary to justify long-term Western support ⁠for ​Ukraine, adding ​that Germany would ​step up ‌its backing in defense and humanitarian ​aid ⁠as Russia intensifies attacks on ⁠Ukraine's ​energy infrastructure ahead of winter.

"What we invest in Ukraine now, we will receive back many times over as dividends in the form of stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and growth," the German chancellor remarked.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In 2025, the two countries traded goods worth around €12 billion ($13 billion).

"Freedom and security are now unleashing forces of progress and resilience on a scale never seen before. This is precisely the stance we are now taking against the autocratic and imperialist actors of this world. We are the world of freedom," Merz added.

At home, Merz has faced increasing pressure to justify Germany's ongoing support for Ukraine. In recent regional elections, political parties opposing sending military aid have performed well.

Merz argued that Russia's war against Ukraine is an attack on democratic values everywhere.

Germany's electricity exports rose in the first three quarters of this year, according to official data released on Friday.

According to the energy association BDEW, Germany has been a net importer of electricity since 2023.

The neighbouring countries Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands, were the most crucial buyers of German electricity in the first nine months of 2026.

Together, they bought about half of all German electricity exports.

According to recent reports, the volume of German electricity exported rose by 25.5% compared with the same period last year, to 48.8 terawatt-hours, while its value increased by 51.3% to €4.3 billion ($4.7 billion). Electricity imports into Germany fell by 13.3% in volume, but at 49.2 terawatt-hours they remained slightly above exports.

While imported electricity cost an average of €116 per megawatt-hour, 39% more than a year earlier, exported electricity from Germany averaged only €87 per megawatt-hour, some 20.6% more than a year earlier.

With a high share of renewable energy sources, wind and solar, Germany tends to offer electricity when supply is high and prices are low, but in times of shortage it has to pay higher prices for imported electricity.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Finance Ministry officials said they are launching a dialogue process, dubbed "Germany 2035," to develop proposals for the future of the country's economy.

Officials want to study how Germany can secure growth and prosperity and what that could look like in terms of fiscal policy.

Finance Minister Lars ​Klingbeil will begin the dialogue process on December ​2, when he welcomes economists from around the world to Berlin.

Additionally, think tanks, research organizations, universities and civil society groups have been asked to host workshops, which would take place in the first half of 2027.

Among 12 economic topics that the ministry seeks to explore are tax and fiscal policy, investment ⁠and ​domestic demand, industrial policy, energy ​and climate transition, foreign trade and sovereignty, and housing ​and local infrastructure.

The dialogue will culminate in a white paper, to be published in 2028, that can provide recommendations for Germany's economic future up to 2035.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A group called "Gen Z Takes Charge" (Gen Z regelt) has called for thousands of young people to demonstrate in many German cities.

The gathering comes almost three weeks after the first major youth protests hit Germany, inspired by the protests that took place in France in the last weeks.

Those protests, which took place on October 31, saw tens of thousands take to the streets across Germany, with crowds remaining largely peaceful, although rioting broke out in several cities, including Frankfurt, later in the evening.

Among the demands of the "Gen Z Takes Charge" group are increased funding for schools, addiction support and psychotherapy, affordable living, opposition to conscription and consistent action on climate change.

Another group, the Federal Pupils' Conference, has also organized its own demonstration at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, with police saying that some 5,000 people have already signed up.

The pupils' conference advocates for improvements in education policy in Germany, including school renovation, school social work, relief for teachers and the inclusion of climate action in curricula.

The demonstrations are set to begin in the morning and run until late afternoon.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier welcomed the Emir of Qatar Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani in Berlin with military honors.

According to recent reports, steinmeier will also host a state banquet for the emir and his delegation in the evening. Al Thani is also expected to meet with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during the day.

The visit comes in the midst of tensions in the Middle East, with the war in Iran likely to be a critical topic in the talks between the two governments. Qatar is presently one of the mediators in the deadlocked conflict between the US and Iran.

Economic and bilateral relations are also expected to take center stage.

On Saturday, the emir will visit Germany's most populous state of North Rhine-Westphalia, where he will be greeted by its state premier Hendrik Wüst at the military section of Cologne/Bonn Konrad Adenauer Airport.

During the visit, Al Thani and North Rhine-Wesphalia leaders will hold an economic conference in the small city of Königswinter, near Bonn, where the Emir will also visit Drachenburg Castle.

Following a political summit on Ukraine in Berlin yesterday, the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce (DIHK) said it would host a German-Ukrainian business forum.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche are expected to be in attendance, along with Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi, among others.

Christian Bruch, deputy chair of the Eastern Committee of the German Economy and chief executive of Siemens Energy, noted German companies are committed to invest in Ukraine, despite Russia's ongoing war and were open to expand their business partnerships.

Bruch noted bilateral trade was expected to rise to around €13 billion ($14.1 billion) in 2026.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

German flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its airport hubs in Frankfurt and Munich, according to a organization letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.

The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa Airlines CEO Jens Ritter and four other managers.

Recent findings suggest that the timeframe of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were apart of a previously revealed downsizing.

In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.

Lufthansa's parent tech giant Lufthansa Group had 67,100 employees in Germany by the end of last year. In the letter seen by news agencies, Lufthansa said financial struggles were the reason behind the planned cuts.

"Lufthansa is right now not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter mentioned, while pointing out that the company operated at a €180 million ($197 million) loss in the first nine months of this year.

In addition, Lufthansa Airlines is now in its third straight year of being unprofitable.

In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

Leaked documents raise new questions about Deutsche Bank's dealings in Russia up to Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, adding to scrutiny over the bank's risk controls and past controversies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US.

Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president mentioned, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen.".

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

According to recent reports, "I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even remarked that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday declared firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back.

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about complications including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

According to recent reports, "You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

It has been revealed that "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets.".

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google unveiled a â¬13bn ($15bn: Â£11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

Google has been contacted for comment.

Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most crucial temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.
  • Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.
  • In a recent development, the Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most crucial temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

In a recent development, the Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

But now there has been a breakthrough.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle.".

In a recent development, only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

It has been revealed that then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!".

In a recent development, nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

According to recent reports, brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go.".

Sources indicate that the researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Sources indicate that digitally fitting the fragments together led to another notable discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

Recent findings suggest that the Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

According to recent reports, using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

According to recent reports, alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

According to recent reports, there is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

Industry observers note that in the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

Greece, however, considers them stolen.

In a recent development, for years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

It has been revealed that the exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, “I do the same I kind of always do.
  • On 7LLVSION, Ridha frequently turned to an obscure Italian semimodular synth, the Grp A4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘I always look for the newest machines.’.

Sources indicate that if you’re wondering how Alex Ridha’s (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his new record 7LLVSION, the answer is simple: It didn’t. That’s not to say Ridha didn’t learn anything from the virtuosic production team of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, but most of the songs on 7LLVSION had been knocking around for some time. And as Ridha is quick to point out, these are not rock songs built for live performance; they’re “battle tested” for clubs and DJ sets. “I was kind of back on the usual kind of thing,” he tells The Verge.

In a recent development, “I do the same I kind of always do. I go make coffee, go in my room, put on the machines, and I’ll start messing around with sounds and build one sound to another and there comes a record,” he indicates. Like previous Boys Noize releases, a lot of 7LLVSION starts with sound design. “It’s kind of tech-driven, in a way,” he says, “because I always look for the newest machines.”.

On 7LLVSION, Ridha frequently turned to an obscure Italian semimodular synth, the Grp A4. “It’s just so powerful, and it sounds so big,” he states. The routing options, dual filters (which he uses in parallel), and built-in sequencer kept leading him to new and inspiring places. Because of that, the A4 ended up on a number of tracks, including “Shut It Down,” “1+1+1,” and “Ycore.”.

“The exciting part is always to, you know, not repeat myself, even with the drum sounds, and try something new that I haven’t tried before,” Ridha indicates. For a few tracks, that meant getting away from the rigid, quantized grooves of techno and opting for a more dynamic, live feeling on tracks like “Shut It Down” and “1+1+1” especially. “Live drums are the new 808,” he says.

He looked to German bands of the ’70s and ’80s for inspiration, like Can, Amon Düül, and Deutsch Amerikanische Freundschaft. He also called out Conny Plank, who produced landmark records by Neu!, Kraftwerk, and Eurythmics. But in general he says, “My goal is to not sound like anything you can point to. You know, I don’t want to be a direct copy.” Instead, he was chasing the sound of “electronic punk.” That means aggressive basslines, driving drums, and stripped-down arrangements that avoid overstuffing the mix with too many instruments.

But it all comes back to the club at the end of the day. “Environment has always been the main thing in my music. I need to have a record that I want to play at the party,” he says, and that meant testing the songs off 7LLVSION extensively in his DJ sets and letting the audience tell him what works and what doesn’t. “The club is the most open and objective situation you can have,” he says. “They don’t know what I’m playing, so they hear something for the first time, and you can just look at someone’s face, or someone’s there in the room to get a cool reaction, and that usually makes me feel good about something or not.”.

Boys Noize is currently touring the world on the festival circuit, and 7LLVSION is available now on most major streaming services.

Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza.
  • Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
  • The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza.

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.

The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

It has been revealed that the US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also declared sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

According to recent reports, the Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.

Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”.

In remarks addressed to Pillay, he mentioned: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”.

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, noted: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”.

He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.

It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.

The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.

The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.

Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

Sources indicate that on Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its strategy to impose sanctions on the ICC.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A fresh draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'.
